summary.text: A 64-year-old woman had repeated unresolved chest-infection presentations despite antibiotics, culminating in pneumonia-associated fulminant septic shock with refractory hypotension, hypothermia and altered mental status. Serial admission observations and blood results showed explicit AKI 3, hyponatraemia, low bicarbonate and elevated inflammatory markers; clotting narrative/table conflict remains review-only.

Deterioration prompted empiric steroids for suspected adrenal insufficiency. CT followed by MRI showed bilateral AH, with low morning cortisol 44 nmol/L and primary adrenal crisis/Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 50 mg QDS, IV antibiotics/fluid and ICU monitoring led to stabilisation; no vasopressor was needed. Oral hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone followed, but adrenal function remained impaired at five months, requiring ongoing replacement.

On day 3, a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) to evaluate dyspnoea and chest pain revealed bilateral pulmonary embolism and a new 34 mm well-defined low-attenuation mass at the site of the previously demonstrated left adrenal gland, most likely representing haemorrhage into the adrenal gland.

An MRI (Figure 2) was done in three days' time, which identified a lesion involving the left adrenal gland; it measured 32 x 31 mm and showed no significant interval change in comparison to the previous study. The patient was initiated on intravenous antibiotics (IV Tazocin) and fluids, received supplemental oxygen, and was started on apixaban for the pulmonary embolism. He did not need any steroids.

An F/U MRI performed approximately three months later confirmed that the left adrenal gland appears much smaller and measured 21 x 13 mm in comparison to 32 x 31 mm in the previous study. A normal right adrenal gland was seen.

summary.text: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD, hypertension, osteoporosis, previous subarachnoid haemorrhages and chronic hyponatremia presented after an unwitnessed fall with amnesia and preceding left chest pain. Suspected infective COPD exacerbation was treated with antibiotics/nebuliser. Admission inflammatory markers were high; ACS was excluded and bronchoscopic endobronchial lesions absent.

Day 3 CTPA identified bilateral pulmonary emboli and a 34 mm probable left adrenal haemorrhage; MRI three days later measured 32 x 31 mm without interval change. Cortisol 579 nmol/L was described as normal, with no overt adrenal insufficiency/crisis; conservative AH management required no steroids/surgery. Tazocin, fluids, oxygen and apixaban were given. MRI about three months later showed 21 x 13 mm left lesion and normal right gland. Respiratory improvement followed by declining baseline function led to home NIV; endocrinology review and six-month MRI remained planned.

summary.text: A 42-year-old man with JAK2-positive essential thrombocythemia diagnosed incidentally during COVID pneumonitis admission about three years earlier, on aspirin and regular losartan for hypertension, developed abrupt moderate 6/10 diffuse abdominal pain after two days of flu-like symptoms. Nausea, lethargy, poor oral intake and altered bowel movements occurred without urinary symptoms. Influenza A nasal PCR was positive, with thrombocytosis, lymphopenia, high neutrophils/CRP and hypokalaemia; blood culture showed no growth.

Non-contrast then contrast CT localised a left adrenal lesion with haemorrhage/infection differential. Endocrine screening showed normal plasma metanephrines, aldosterone 380 pmol/L and renin 5.2 nmol/L/hr with ratio 73 interpreted against primary aldosteronism; cortisol/ACTH and infectious screening results were not reported. IV antibiotics, oseltamivir, potassium replacement and supportive care were given; no AH-specific treatment was needed. Post-discharge MRI showed stable 2.7 x 2.5 cm lipid-rich haemorrhagic adenoma; later endocrine review was asymptomatic, six-month MRI stable without malignancy, and renal MRA showed no stenosis. Outpatient hormonal surveillance continued; imaging diagnosis lacked tissue verification.
